hook.support: You got your first job. Now there are tax forms. TFN. myGov. Tax return. It sounds hard. It isn’t. Most of it is one form and one app.
hook.core: First job, first payslip, and suddenly there are new words everywhere: TFN, tax-free threshold, myGov, tax return. It sounds scary. It isn’t. Most of it comes down to one form at the start and one tax return a year. Get them right and you might even get money back.
hook.extend: Tax arrives with your first job. There’s a form to fill in, tax taken from every pay, and a return to lodge each year. The forms are made for ordinary people. Once you can read them, you can avoid the mistakes that turn a refund into a bill.

why.support: Get your tax right and you keep more of your money. Get it wrong and you can owe money.
why.core: Tax mistakes cost real money: a surprise bill, or a refund you never claim. Reading the forms properly means you pay the right amount and nothing more.
why.extend: Tax forms are some of the most common official texts you’ll deal with as an adult. Reading them well protects you from debts, missed refunds and scams.

articles.title: Your first tax year

body.support:
Tax is money you pay to the government from what you earn. Here is what to do.

**1. Get a TFN.** A **tax file number** is your own number for tax. You get it from the **ATO**. It is free. Keep it private. Don’t post it or text it.

**2. Fill in the TFN form.** When you start a job, your boss gives you a form. It asks for your TFN. It also asks: **do you want to claim the tax-free threshold?**

The first **$18,200** you earn in a year has no tax. If you have **one** job, you usually say yes. If you have **two** jobs, say yes for **one** job only. If you say yes for both, you could owe money later.

**3. Check your payslip.** It shows how much tax your boss took out.

**4. Do your tax return.** Each year, between **1 July and 31 October**, you do a **tax return**. You can do it on **myGov**. You might get a **refund**.

**Watch out:** don’t click links in texts that say they are from the ATO. Go to myGov yourself.
body.core:
Tax is money the government collects from what you earn. It pays for things like hospitals, schools and roads. Here’s how it works in your first job.

**1. Get a tax file number (TFN).** Your TFN is your personal number for tax. You apply to the **Australian Taxation Office (ATO)**, and it’s free. Keep it private: never post it, text it to strangers or put it on a resume.

**2. Fill in a TFN declaration.** When you start a job, you give your employer a **TFN declaration**. It asks for your TFN, your details, and whether you want to **claim the tax-free threshold**.

The **tax-free threshold** is the first **$18,200** you earn in a financial year. You don’t pay tax on it. If you have one job, you usually claim it. If you have **two jobs at the same time**, the ATO says to generally claim it from **one** employer only, usually the one that pays you the most. Claim it from both, and each one takes out too little tax. Then you could get a **tax bill** at the end of the year.

**3. Check your payslips.** Each payslip shows the tax your employer **withheld** (kept back and sent to the ATO for you).

**4. Lodge your tax return.** The financial year runs from 1 July to 30 June. Between **1 July and 31 October**, you lodge a **tax return**, usually online through **myGov**. It works out whether you paid the right amount. If too much was taken, you get a **refund**.

**Scam warning:** scammers pretend to be the ATO. Don’t click links in texts or emails about tax. Log in to myGov yourself.
body.extend:
Tax is the government’s share of what you earn, collected to fund public services. Your first job brings three tax documents into your life.

**1. Tax file number (TFN).** Your unique identifier with the **Australian Taxation Office (ATO)**. It’s free, and it’s valuable to identity thieves, so keep it private.

**2. TFN declaration.** You give this form to each new employer. The key decision is whether to **claim the tax-free threshold**: the first **$18,200** of income each financial year, on which no tax is payable. With one job, you usually claim it. With **two or more jobs at once**, the ATO advises you generally claim it from **one** payer only, usually the highest-paying. If you claim it from both, each employer assumes you’re entitled to the full threshold and **withholds** too little, so you can end the year with a **tax debt**.

**3. Tax return.** The financial year ends on 30 June. Between **1 July and 31 October**, you lodge a return, usually through myTax via **myGov**. Your employers report your income to the ATO, so much of the return is pre-filled. You can also claim legitimate work-related **deductions**, if you kept records. The return reconciles what was withheld with what you owe, producing a **refund** or a bill.

Tax forms use precise wording, and small choices (a tick in one box) have real consequences months later. Read every question, and infer what each choice will mean for you. And treat any unexpected message “from the ATO” with suspicion: log in to myGov yourself rather than following a link.

caseStudies.title: Two jobs, one threshold

body.support:
Lots of young people have two jobs. Maybe a café on weekends and a shop after school.

Each new boss gives you a TFN form. Each form asks: claim the tax-free threshold?

The **ATO** says: with two jobs at the same time, you usually claim it from **one** job only. Pick the one that pays you more.

If you claim it from **both**, each boss takes out too little tax. At tax time, you could owe the ATO money.

You can fix it. Give one boss a new form to stop claiming it there.
body.core:
Lots of young Australians work two casual jobs at once: a café on weekends, a supermarket after school. Each employer gives you a TFN declaration, and each one asks the same question: **do you want to claim the tax-free threshold?**

It’s easy to tick **yes** both times. But the **Australian Taxation Office (ATO)** says that if you have more than one payer at the same time, you should generally claim the threshold from **one** payer only, usually the one who pays you the most.

Here’s why. Each employer works out your tax as if theirs is your only job. If both think you get the first $18,200 tax-free, each takes out too little tax. When you lodge your tax return, the ATO adds both jobs together, and you could get a **tax bill**.

If you’ve already ticked yes twice, you can fix it. The ATO says to give one employer a withholding declaration to stop claiming the threshold there.
body.extend:
Many young people work two casual jobs. Each new employer asks them to fill in a TFN declaration with the same question: **do you want to claim the tax-free threshold from this payer?**

The **Australian Taxation Office** says that if you have more than one payer at the same time, you should generally claim the threshold from **one** payer only. That’s usually the one paying the most. If your total income will be over $18,200, the other payers should take out tax at the higher “no tax-free threshold” rate.

The logic is simple once you see how withholding works. Each employer works out your tax as if theirs is your only job. If both use the full $18,200 threshold, too little tax is withheld overall. When the ATO adds up your income at tax time, the gap becomes a **debt**.

The fix is another form: a withholding declaration that stops the threshold at one employer. The bigger lesson is that one tick on an official form can matter months later. Read the question, think about what it means for you, and check the ATO’s advice when you’re unsure.

model.text:
**Tax for your first job: the 4 things to know**

**1. Get a TFN.** It’s your number for tax. It’s free from the ATO. Keep it private.

**2. Fill in the TFN form.** Your boss gives you one. It asks if you want the tax-free threshold. That means no tax on the first $18,200 you earn in a year.

**3. Two jobs?** Tick yes for one job only, the one that pays more. Tick yes on both and you could get a tax bill.

**4. Do your tax return.** Between 1 July and 31 October, on myGov. You might get money back!

**Never** click a link in a text about tax. Log in to myGov yourself.

teacher.overview: Students learn the three tax documents of a first job (TFN, TFN declaration, tax return), the tax-free threshold and the two-jobs rule, and how to spot tax scams. They annotate a simplified TFN declaration, sort smart moves from tax traps, and write a tax guide for a friend. The case study is the ATO’s advice on claiming the tax-free threshold from one payer only when working two jobs.
prep: Optional: print a blank TFN declaration from the ATO website so students can see the real form (never collect a completed one).
Check the ATO website is reachable for the Level Up.
Check the current tax-free threshold and lodgement dates on the ATO site before teaching.

teacher.answers:
**Annotation:** 1 TFN (private); 2 personal details (match ID); 3 residency (changes tax rates); 4 tax-free threshold (yes for one job only); 5 study or training loan (extra withheld); 6 declaration (a promise; sign last).

**Sort:** TFN to new boss — smart; posting TFN — trap; threshold on both jobs — trap; lodging in September — smart; clicking refund link — trap; keeping receipts for boots — smart.

**Case study:** both forms ask the same question, so people tick yes twice; each employer withholds too little and a bill can result; the ATO says to claim from one payer only (usually the highest-paying) and lodge a withholding declaration with the other.

realityCheck: **Never collect students’ TFNs** or completed forms. Use the simplified example and blank official forms only.
**Thresholds and dates can change.** Check the ATO website each year before teaching; the course points students to the ATO for current figures.
**Some students already have tax problems** (a bill, a missing payslip). Point them to the ATO or the free Tax Help program rather than giving individual advice.
**Residency is sensitive.** Don’t ask students about visa or residency status in class.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Students with jobs bring real questions, and many go home and check their own TFN declarations.
